area: Area VII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain, demonstrate from the right seat and teach a soft-field takeoff and climb at VX or VY ±5 knots, simulate a soft field safely on a paved runway, and spot, explain and fix the soft-field errors learners make most.
why: Soft-field technique is what gets an airplane off tall grass, sand, mud or snow before the surface drag stops it, and it leans on ground effect at speeds below a safe climb speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. The first accident profile in the RMH is a near-gross-weight departure from a wet turf strip that ended in 100-foot trees with the stall warning sounding [[30:64|RMH C-1]]. The AFH soft-field section gives the pilot's procedure but no instructor notes, so how you teach it, and how you fake a soft field on pavement, is up to you.

prereading.what: Ground effect on takeoff, the soft/rough-field takeoff and its common errors, rejected takeoff and engine failure.
prereading.label: AFH 6-10 to 6-14

prereading.what: Ground effect: the induced drag numbers by wing height and what happens leaving it.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-11 to 5-12

prereading.what: The four left-turning elements: torque reaction, corkscrew slipstream, gyroscopic action and P-factor.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-30 to 5-32

prereading.what: Region of reversed command after a soft-field lift-off, runway surface and slope, wind and weight effects.
prereading.label: PHAK 11-12 to 11-16

prereading.what: Managing risk while teaching takeoffs, including the AIH's only soft-field teaching note.
prereading.label: AIH 10-7 to 10-8

prereading.what: Accident profile 1: a heavy airplane, a wet turf runway and 100-foot trees.
prereading.label: RMH C-1 to C-2

prereading.what: Tailwheel soft-field takeoff: elevator full up while taxiing on, tail kept low.
prereading.label: AFH 14-3 to 14-4

warmup: Think first: the nearest grass strip is an hour away, so your learner's first soft-field takeoffs will be on smooth pavement. The whole point of the technique is drag from the surface. What can a paved runway teach about it, what can it not teach, and what new risk does a nose-high roll on fast-accelerating pavement add?

key_terms.def: A takeoff technique that gets the airplane airborne as quickly as possible to escape drag from tall grass, soft sand, mud or snow, using ground effect to reduce landing gear drag [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Moving the support of the airplane's weight from the wheels to the wings as early as possible by holding a relatively high angle of attack through the roll [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Improved performance close to the ground, normally up to one wingspan high, from reduced upwash, downwash and wingtip vortices and so less induced drag [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Drag that comes from the wing's work of producing lift; it is greatest at high angles of attack, so it dominates at low speed [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].
Best angle of climb speed: the greatest gain in altitude for a given distance over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Best rate of climb speed: the greatest gain in altitude per unit of time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
The slow side of the power required curve, where flying slower needs more power, not less [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Weight concentrated on the nosewheel during the takeoff or landing roll, so the airplane can pivot on the nosewheel and lose directional control [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].
Left yaw at high angle of attack because the downswinging propeller blade takes a bigger bite than the upswinging one [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
The spiral of propeller wash that strikes the vertical fin and yaws the airplane; strongest at high propeller speed and low forward speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
The airplane's tendency to roll opposite the propeller's rotation; on the ground it presses the left wheel down and adds friction there [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
An optical illusion over snow, dust, sand, mud flats or glassy water that removes depth and contrast, so a pilot cannot judge distance or tell climbing from level flight [[34:170|AIM 7-6-14]].

chunks.title: The maneuver, its purpose and the standard you hold

body.p: Purpose: the soft-field technique gets the airplane airborne as quickly as possible to get rid of the drag from tall grass, soft sand, mud and snow, and it may also have to climb over an obstacle [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. The same technique fits a rough field, where getting off early keeps the landing gear from being damaged [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

Teach early that it is not a short-field takeoff. On a short field with a firm surface, the airplane rolls with its full weight on the main wheels in a low-drag attitude [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. On a soft field, the AFH calls the correct procedure quite different: the weight goes onto the wings as fast as possible [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

bullets: Flaps, if the manufacturer recommends them, go down before the takeoff starts [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Keep moving with enough power while lining up; stopping in mud or snow can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Apply takeoff power smoothly and as rapidly as the engine will accept without faltering [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Use enough back-elevator pressure to set a positive angle of attack and take weight off the nosewheel [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Hold that nose-high attitude; the airplane flies itself off at an airspeed slower than a safe climb speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Gently lower the nose with the wheels just clear and stay in ground effect until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Climb at VX until any obstacle is cleared, then VY; retract gear and flaps after a positive rate at VY [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

head: Item
Private ACS (your learner)
Flight Instructor ACS (you)
rows: Climb pitch after leaving ground effect
Climb to a safe maneuvering altitude
Demonstrate it and explain it at the same time, and analyze and correct common errors (ACS AI.VII.C Skills, S15)

body.p: This lesson assumes the normal takeoff basics from Lesson AI.VII.A (rotation picture, attitude-hold-check, the crosswind roll). Here you add what is different on a soft surface.

check.q: Your POH lists VX as 59 knots and trees stand past the end of the strip. What airspeed windows apply to your learner on the private checkride and to you on the CFI checkride?
check.a: Learner: 54 to 69 knots (+10/-5, ACS PA.IV.C.S10). You: 54 to 64 knots (±5, ACS AI.VII.C.S10).

chunks.title: Weight from wheels to wings, and the runway surface

body.p: Importance of weight transfer: a soft surface, or long wet grass, cuts acceleration so much that a normal takeoff technique may never reach takeoff speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Tires sink into soft, grassy or muddy runways, and mud, snow or standing water act as obstructions that slow the airplane [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

How the weight moves: with the nose held high through the whole run, the wings carry more and more of the weight as speed and lift build. That cuts the drag from bumps and from the surface gripping the tires [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Flaps, when the manufacturer recommends them, add lift so the transfer starts even earlier [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

Runway surface/condition: performance charts usually assume a paved, level, smooth, dry runway, and any surface that is not hard and smooth lengthens the ground roll [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. The Chart Supplement lists each runway's surface [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]] and its slope; an upslope slows acceleration further [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. The PHAK sample chart corrects only for a dry grass runway, adding 15% of the ground roll figure [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. A rough field calls for the same technique to spare the landing gear [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

callout.text: The opposite mistake is pinning the nosewheel down with forward elevator. That puts excessive pressure on the nosewheel and can cause wheelbarrowing [[24:144|AFH 6-12]], where the airplane tends to swerve or pivot on the nosewheel [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

body.p: Tailwheel learners: keep the tail very low through the roll. That keeps the built-in positive angle of attack and fights any tendency to nose over in soft spots, tall grass or deep snow [[24:290|AFH 14-4]].

callout.text: Application: a picture that works on the ground is 'every pound the wings carry is a pound the tires are not dragging through the mud.' Then ask the learner what happens to that drag the moment the nosewheel touches back down.

check.q: A learner asks why we raise the nose early on a soft field when a short-field takeoff keeps it low until VX. Your short answer?
check.a: On a firm short field the low-drag attitude gives the best acceleration [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. On a soft field the surface drag is the problem, so the nose-high attitude moves weight onto the wings and off the wheels as early as possible [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

chunks.title: Ground effect: the tool that makes it work

body.p: Ground effect is improved performance very close to the ground, normally up to one wingspan high. It matters most at a constant attitude, low airspeed and low altitude, exactly the soft-field lift-off [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. The ground restricts the wing's upwash, downwash and wingtip vortices, so induced drag drops [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].

head: Wing height above the surface
Cut in induced drag (PHAK)
AFH rounding
rows: The normal upper limit of ground effect [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]

body.p: The instruments fool you a little: higher static pressure makes the airspeed indicator and altimeter read slightly low, and the VSI usually shows a descent [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. So the airplane can be airborne at an indicated airspeed below what it normally needs [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].

bullets: Leaving ground effect, the airplane needs more angle of attack for the same lift [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Induced drag and thrust required go up [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
The nose tends to pitch up, because downwash at the tail increases [[24:142|AFH 6-10]], and stability decreases [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].
The indicated airspeed rises as static source pressure drops [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

body.p: The ACS asks you to lift off at the lowest possible airspeed and remain in ground effect while accelerating to VX or VY (ACS AI.VII.C.S9). The AFH explains why: from an unsatisfactory surface, put as much weight on the wings as possible and use ground effect before reaching true flying speed, then reduce the angle of attack to gain normal airspeed before flying out of ground effect [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

callout.text: Right after lift-off, the airplane tends to settle back onto the surface while it leaves ground effect, even at full power. It must stay in ground effect until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

check.q: Your airplane has a 35-foot wingspan. At what wing height does the PHAK give a 47.6 percent cut in induced drag?

chunks.title: VX, VY and the climb out of ground effect

head: Speed
What it gives
When, after a soft-field takeoff
rows: Greatest altitude gain for the distance over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
When an obstacle must be cleared: climb at VX until it is cleared [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Greatest altitude gain per unit of time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
Once clear of obstacles, or when there are none; gear and flaps come up at VY [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]

body.p: VX is usually slightly less than VY, and both come from the AFM/POH [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. With altitude, VX increases and VY decreases until they meet at the absolute ceiling [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. In some airplanes a 5-knot error from the recommended speed costs a lot of climb, which is why the standard is tight [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

The soft-field danger zone is the gap between 'airborne' and 'able to climb.' The airplane may seem able to take off below the recommended speed, but climbing out of ground effect too slow gives much less climb than VY or even VX. Hot, high or heavy, it may lift off and still not climb out of ground effect [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

callout.text: Teach the level-off as a short wait, not a hover: in ground effect the airplane accelerates fast, and when the airspeed reaches VX the pitch goes to the VX or VY attitude. Use the AFH order: attitude on the horizon first, then a glance at the airspeed [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

check.q: No obstacles past the end of a long turf strip. Your learner plans to hold VX all the way to pattern altitude 'to be safe.' What do you teach?
check.a: VX is for clearing obstacles; without one, accelerate in ground effect and climb at VY, which gives the most altitude per unit of time [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

chunks.title: Configuration: flaps, gear, power and mixture

bullets: Flaps: set before the roll starts, only if the manufacturer recommends them, for extra lift and early weight transfer [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Never exceed the POH takeoff flap setting [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].

Retracting: after a positive rate of climb and acceleration to VY, retract gear and flaps; with an obstacle, climb at VX until clear, then set VY and retract [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Never retract gear or flaps before a positive rate of climb [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].
Wet snow or slush on the strip: do not retract the gear right away, so the slush can air-dry [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Raising flaps in steps: the AFH advises increments to avoid a sudden loss of lift and settling, in its short-field section [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. It fits the slow soft-field climb too (application).
Power: takeoff power for the run and climb; reduce to normal climb power after gear and flaps are up [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Mixture: the PHAK sample chart says to lean for maximum rpm in a full-throttle static runup before takeoff from fields above 3,000 feet [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Follow your POH.

callout.text: Teaching risk: a learner who reaches for the flap switch in ground effect is looking inside at the worst moment. The AFH wants eyes outside, not on the gear or flap controls, until obstacles are cleared [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

check.q: Your learner wants to start flaps up while still in ground effect 'to cut drag and accelerate faster.' What is wrong with that?
check.a: Gear and flaps come up only after a positive rate of climb and VY [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], never before a positive rate of climb [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]]. Near the ground, losing flap lift can let the airplane settle [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

chunks.title: Left-turning tendencies in a nose-high, full-power roll

body.p: The soft-field roll is full power, low speed and a high angle of attack all at once, so all four left-turning elements are active: torque reaction, the corkscrew slipstream, gyroscopic action and P-factor [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

head: Element
Why it is strong in a soft-field roll
rows: On the ground it presses the left side down, so the left tire carries more weight and friction, adding a turn to the left. Its size depends on engine power, propeller size and rpm, airplane size and the condition of the ground surface [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
At high propeller speed and low forward speed the spiral is compact and pushes hard on the fin. It weakens as speed builds [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
Any pitching makes a yawing moment, so the pilot uses elevator and rudder together [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. Rapid pitch changes give proportionate changes in torque effects [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
At a high angle of attack the downswinging blade bites harder, moving the thrust center right and yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

body.p: What the learner feels: heavy right rudder as power comes in with the nose up, and changing rudder needs as the nose is lowered in ground effect and raised again for the climb (application). Steer with rudder, not brakes: braking slows acceleration, lengthens the takeoff and can cause severe swerving [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]. Poor directional control is on the AFH soft-field error list [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

callout.text: Ask for pressure, not movement. The AFH wants the learner to sense resistance and wait for the airplane's reaction instead of moving the controls through wide ranges [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

check.q: Which of the PHAK's variables for the torque turning moment on the ground ties most directly to a soft field?
check.a: The condition of the ground surface [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. More tire drag on the left wheel means a stronger pull to the left.

chunks.title: Air, wind and choosing the strip

body.p: Atmospheric conditions: high elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity all raise density altitude, and thin air cuts engine power, propeller thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. The airplane lifts off at the same indicated airspeed but a higher true airspeed, so the roll gets longer [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]], and on a soft field every extra foot of roll is spent fighting surface drag.

head: Change
Effect on takeoff distance
Source
rows: Sample chart: each 9 knots of headwind
Sample chart: each 2 knots of tailwind, up to 10 knots
Add 15% of the ground roll figure

body.p: Tailwind: a tailwind makes the airplane reach a higher groundspeed to get to lift-off airspeed [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. Before any tailwind takeoff, confirm the POH/AFM approves it and that performance and runway length are enough [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

Gusts: in strong, gusty wind the AFH wants an extra margin of speed before leaving the ground, because a lull at normal takeoff speed can cost positive control or cause a stall [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. That pulls against 'lowest possible airspeed' (see cfi_notes).

Selection of runway: the PIC must know the runway lengths and the takeoff and landing distance data for the conditions [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. Takeoffs grow more hazardous as calculated performance approaches the available runway length [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. Leave room to stop: takeoff plus landing ground roll estimates the runway needed to accelerate and stop [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Pilot capability is its own limit: the RMH sample minimums list a 2,500-foot shortest runway [[30:16|RMH 2-4]], and an unfamiliar airport calls for adding at least 500 feet [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

Use the RMH accident profile as your case study. A pilot near maximum gross weight with three passengers departed a 3,100-foot turf runway with 3-inch or higher wet grass and 100-foot trees at the end. The POH showed about 1,700 feet over a 50-foot obstacle from a hard surface and had no data for wet turf or a 100-foot obstacle. The stall warning sounded just before the airplane hit the trees [[30:64|RMH C-1]]. The RMH's mitigation: fly solo to the nearby towered airport, Eugene, and board the passengers there [[30:65|RMH C-2]].

Reading the chart excerpt: (Pvt) after a name means private use, not open to the public [[2:64|Chart Users' Guide p.64]]. Under the name come the elevation in feet and the length of the longest runway in hundreds of feet, which may be more than the usable length [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p.15]]. Towered airports and their data are blue; others are magenta [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p.15]].

callout.text: Application: when the POH has no number for the surface you face, as in the RMH case [[30:64|RMH C-1]], teach learners to treat that as a reason for more margin, not as permission to guess optimistically.

check.q: Using the PHAK sample chart notes, what correction do you apply for an 8-knot tailwind on a paved runway?
check.a: 10% for each 2 knots: 8 / 2 = 4, so add 40% to the distances [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

chunks.title: Before the roll: checklists, radios, runway, wind and a rolling start

bullets: Checklists: finish the run-up and before-takeoff checklist before taxiing onto the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]], on firm ground if you can (application), because the soft-field lineup does not stop [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Radio: on CTAF, self-announce with the airport name at the start and end of the call [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]], and stay alert for arrivals from the opposite direction [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

Verify the runway: set the heading bug to the runway heading and check heading against runway before adding power [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. At a field with paved and turf runways, check the surface in the Chart Supplement [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

Wind: the large end of a wind cone points into the wind [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]]; a sock also shows speed and gusts [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. With no indicator, use smoke, dust or patterns on water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

Controls for wind while taxiing: quartering headwind, upwind aileron up; quartering tailwind, elevator down and upwind aileron down [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. A tailwheel airplane taxiing onto a soft runway at high power usually wants the elevator full up [[24:290|AFH 14-4]].
Clear the area and roll on without stopping: keep the airplane moving with enough power while lining up [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Not clearing the area is on the soft-field error list [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

Takeoff power and instruments: power smoothly and as rapidly as the engine will accept without faltering [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], then cross-check the engine instruments; skipping that cross-check after applying power is a listed error [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

body.p: Towered fields: line up and wait is not a takeoff clearance [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]], and you need the takeoff clearance before beginning the roll [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5]]. On a really soft surface, holding short until you are cleared for takeoff lets you roll on without stopping (application). If a clearance says 'immediate' and that would hurt your operation, you may refuse it [[33:285|AIM 4-4-13]].

callout.text: Do the teaching before you call the tower or announce on CTAF: airspeeds, pitch attitudes, visual references, control inputs and engine numbers. Do not discuss technique while entering the runway [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

check.q: Why would you hold short rather than accept 'line up and wait' on a muddy runway?
check.a: The soft-field lineup should not stop, since stopping in mud or snow can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], and line up and wait is not a takeoff clearance [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]]. Waiting for the takeoff clearance off the runway lets you roll on and go (application).

body.p: On the checkride you fly from the right seat and talk at the same time. Keep each callout short; the airplane gets busy fast.

head: Step
What you do
What you say
rows: Keep moving with enough power, controls set for the wind, back pressure held [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Smoothly and as rapidly as the engine accepts; cross-check the gauges [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]
Enough back pressure for a positive angle of attack and a light nosewheel [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Keep the nose-high attitude so the wings take the weight as speed builds [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
'Hold it steady; it will fly itself off.'
Airborne below a safe climb speed; gently lower the nose with the wheels just clear [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
'We're flying. Ease the nose down, stay low.'
Stay in ground effect until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]; hold the wind correction
'A few feet up, let it build to VX.'
VX attitude if there is an obstacle, then VY; expect the pitch-up as you leave ground effect [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]
'VX attitude. Watch it want to pitch up.'
Positive rate and VY, then gear and flaps, then climb power [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
'Positive rate, VY, flaps up, climb power.'
Two points ahead aligned with the runway; check ground track often in a crosswind [[24:135|AFH 6-3]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]
'Two points lined up, crab for the wind.'

body.p: Maintain the attitude, do not set it once. S8 asks you to 'establish and maintain' a pitch attitude that transfers the weight as rapidly as possible (ACS AI.VII.C.S8). Too little back pressure early is the first error on the AFH list after planning and clearing [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

Noise abatement: procedures come from the Chart Supplement, local publications, handouts, safety briefings and the tower; if you do not know them, ask the tower [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Many grass strips sit next to homes, so fly as quietly and safely as possible [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

callout.text: Roll, light, hold, low, build, climb: keep it Rolling, make the nosewheel Light, Hold the attitude, stay Low after lift-off, Build to VX, then Climb.

check.q: In your demonstration, what tells you the airplane is 'flying itself off' rather than being pulled off?
check.a: The attitude stays constant and lift builds with speed until the wheels leave on their own [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Pulling it off with extra back pressure raises the pitch and may delay the takeoff or settle it back [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

chunks.title: Crosswind, windshear and wake on a soft field

body.p: Crosswind: start the roll with full aileron into the wind, and expect slower early acceleration from the deflected controls [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]. Hold enough aileron to keep the upwind wing down so the airplane sideslips into the wind enough to stop drift right after lift-off [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. When the main wheels leave the ground, nothing stops the sideways drift any more [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]. A settle-back while drifting is what loads the gear sideways [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].

callout.text: The one FAA teaching note for this maneuver: during soft-field takeoffs, monitor drift while the learner tries to stay in ground effect, do not let it grow beyond the learner's control, and watch pitch and airspeed the whole time [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

body.p: Windshear: low-level windshear is commonly tied to fronts, thunderstorms, temperature inversions and strong upper winds [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A headwind turning to a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Microburst clues are an intense rain shaft at the surface with virga at cloud base, and often only a ring of blowing dust [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

On the roll, slower than normal airspeed build-up may be the only sign of windshear [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]. On a soft field the build-up is slow anyway, so that cue is hidden (application). The decision has to be made before the roll: if convective weather is near, wait.

Wake turbulence: departing behind a larger aircraft, note its rotation point, rotate before it and climb above its path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. A soft-field takeoff deliberately stays low in ground effect, so that plan may not work (application). After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, wait at least 2 minutes, especially in light quartering wind [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Small airplanes should stay out of three rotor diameters of a helicopter in a slow hover taxi or hover, and use caution behind departing or landing helicopters [[34:153|AIM 7-4-7]].

check.q: Why is the AWH's best on-the-roll windshear clue hard to use on a soft field?
check.a: The clue is slower than normal airspeed build-up [[28:270|AWH 22-15]], and a soft surface already slows acceleration [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Application: decide about nearby storms before the roll.

chunks.title: Rejected takeoff, engine failure and the low, slow trap

body.p: Rejected takeoff: inadequate acceleration is one of the listed reasons [[24:146|AFH 6-14]], and on a soft field it is the likely one. Pick the point where you must be airborne; if you reach it on the wheels, act at once: power to idle, maximum braking while keeping directional control [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Braking effectiveness depends on the surface [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]], and no source gives stopping distances for wet grass or mud (see gaps).

Potential engine failure in takeoff/climb phase: at climb pitch without power the airplane is at or near a stalling angle of attack, and you may still be holding right rudder. Lower the nose at once, coordinate, and glide toward a landing area, preferably straight ahead; do not try a turn back unless trained for it with enough altitude [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. For learners and low-time pilots a turn back is an unacceptable risk [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

Low altitude maneuvering, stall: forcing the airplane off with too much back pressure can raise the angle of attack enough to settle it back or stall it [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. If the pilot climbs out of ground effect before reaching normal climb pitch and airspeed, the airplane can enter the region of reversed command at a dangerously low altitude, unable to climb even at full power. The only fix is to lower the nose, which costs altitude [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

Spin: 60 percent of stall/spin accidents happened during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. CFIT: it often follows flight at high density altitude or flying too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]], and the RMH profile ended in trees at the end of a turf runway [[30:64|RMH C-1]].

callout.text: Simulated engine failures done wrong have caused real emergencies and accidents [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Make sure one person clearly has the throttle, and end the simulation as soon as the outcome is clear [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Never simulate one while the airplane is still in ground effect below VX (application).

check.q: Your learner lifts off at 45 knots (VX 59) and pitches straight to the VX climb attitude. At full power the airplane will not climb. What has happened, and what is the only way out?
check.a: It left ground effect too slow and is in the region of reversed command. The only recourse is to lower the pitch to gain airspeed, losing altitude [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

body.p: Collision hazards: in an AIH study most midair collisions happened in good daylight visibility at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet, and an instructor was aboard in 37 percent [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Before entering a runway, the instructor makes sure there is enough spacing from landing and departing aircraft [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. A soft-field lineup does not stop, so the scan for final and the runway must be done before you start rolling on (application). In a tailwheel airplane the cowling can block the view ahead on the ground [[24:289|AFH 14-3]].

Distractions and task prioritization: during a takeoff the learner's attention is almost all on flying, and anything you say may not be heard or processed [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Small problems become accidents when the pilot turns to the problem and neglects control of the aircraft, and in overload the answer is to stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

Loss of situational awareness: a novice often fixates on pitch attitude or the airspeed indicator and neglects bank [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. In the soft-field level-off that shows up as drift or a wing slowly dropping a few feet above the ground.

Disorientation: flat light, over snow, dust, sand or mud flats, removes depth perception and contrast and can make level flight feel like climbing or descending [[34:170|AIM 7-6-14]]. Holding the wheels a few feet above a snow-covered strip is exactly where that matters (application).

callout.text: Model the sterile flight deck: the AIH says the airline rule holds true for the entire aviation community, and instructors should model it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. On a soft-field takeoff, your only words after the roll starts should be short prompts.

check.q: Why should the clearing scan be finished earlier on a soft-field takeoff than on a normal one?
check.a: Because the airplane keeps moving onto the runway and into the roll without stopping [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], so there is no pause on the centerline to look again (application). The instructor ensures spacing before entering the runway [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

chunks.title: How to teach it, and how to simulate a soft field on pavement

body.p: Where it fits: learners go from simple to complex, so the normal landing is mastered before short-field and soft-field landings [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. Apply the same order to takeoffs: a solid normal takeoff first. Then teach the soft-field takeoff known-to-unknown, as a change to the normal takeoff the learner already flies [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

bullets: On the ground: cover the airspeeds, pitch attitudes, visual references, control inputs and engine numbers before you call the tower or announce on CTAF [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Brief the abort point [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] and the engine-failure plan.

Your demonstration: fly it exactly the way the learner should practice it, explaining power settings and attitudes as you go [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Have the learner follow through lightly to feel the pressures [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
Their turn: one short prompt at a time. Watch drift, pitch and airspeed throughout, and do not let drift grow past what the learner can handle [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Afterward: discuss the hazards and what the learner saw in detail on the ground [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

body.p: Make it realistic: the AIH wants takeoff scenarios that mimic what the learner will meet outside training, without creating an unsafe climb rate or excessive pitch attitude. For an obstacle, name a realistic point where an imaginary one stands [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Simulating a soft field on pavement. The sources do not describe a method, so everything in this list is application, built on the AFH procedure and the AIH limits above:

bullets: Brief it as 'this runway is soft': no stopping on the centerline, back pressure from the moment you roll on, and lift-off at the lowest possible airspeed.
Expect everything to happen sooner. Pavement does not hold the wheels back, so the nosewheel comes up and the airplane lifts off earlier than on grass.
Set a pitch limit before the flight. A nose held too high on smooth pavement is the AIH's 'excessive pitch attitude' [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]; check your POH for any tail clearance concern.
Use a long runway with a quiet pattern, so the level-off in ground effect has room and no one is behind you.
Add an imaginary obstacle at a realistic point so the VX climb has a purpose [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Say what pavement cannot teach: the feel of drag, the risk of bogging down and grass-specific performance. Plan a real turf strip once the learner is consistent, with the POH numbers worked first.

callout.text: Guard the controls close to the ground. If you must take over, say 'I have the flight controls' calmly; an anxious learner can be very strong [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Settling back while drifting at low speed is the outcome you are guarding against [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].

check.q: On pavement your learner's nose rises so high that you lose sight of the runway ahead over the cowling. What does the AIH guidance tell you to do?
check.a: Lower it to a reasonable attitude. A training scenario must not create an excessive pitch attitude, and the instructor watches pitch and airspeed throughout the soft-field takeoff [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

body.p: These are the AFH's soft-field takeoff errors [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. The 'what you see' and 'fix' columns come from the AFH text around them.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: The learner cannot state a ground roll or an abort point
Work the chart, add the surface correction, set the abort point [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]
Rolls onto the runway without a look at final
Scan final and the runway before you start rolling on [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Nosewheel stays loaded; slow acceleration in the grass
Back pressure as the roll starts for a positive angle of attack [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Eyes stay outside after full power
Add a gauge callout right after power comes in [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
Nose wanders left as the nose rises; brake use
Rudder pressure for the left-turning effects, no brakes [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
Wheels well above the ground, airspeed still below VX
Lower the nose to stay in ground effect [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Abrupt or excessive elevator at the level-off
A shove forward; the airplane dips toward the surface
Gently lower the nose with the wheels clear [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Letting it mush or settle back
Hold a steady attitude; it settles easily while leaving ground effect [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Climbing out of ground effect too slow
Shallow climb or no climb below VX
Stay in ground effect until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]
Not anticipating the pitch-up leaving ground effect
Nose rises and airspeed decays in the first feet of climb
Expect the pitch-up from increased tail downwash [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]

body.p: Figure 6-9 comes from the AFH short-field section, but it shows the same chain a soft-field learner falls into by climbing out early: low airspeed lift-off, a shallow climb below VX, then settling back [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

On the checkride the examiner may fly a simulated error as your 'learner.' Say what you saw, the likely cause and the fix, then demonstrate it and let them try again; the AIH treats this as reteaching, demonstrate, practice, evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: Right after lift-off your learner's airplane drops back and touches the grass, then lifts off again. Name two errors from the AFH list that can cause this.
check.a: Abrupt or excessive elevator while leveling off, or letting the airplane mush or settle after lift-off [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

f1.caption: Figure 6-10. Soft-field takeoff.
f1.alt: Five airplanes on a grass strip, left to right: accelerate (inset shows the elevator), raise nose-wheel as soon as possible (inset shows the elevator raised), lift off, level off in ground effect, accelerate in ground effect to VX or VY.

f2.caption: Figure 6-7. Takeoff in ground effect area.
f2.alt: Airplanes along a runway labeled: ground effect decreases induced drag; airplane may fly at lower indicated airspeed; accelerate in ground effect to VX or VY; ground effect decreases quickly with height; ground effect is negligible when height is equal to wingspan.

f3.caption: Figure 5-47. Torque reaction. Figure 5-48. Corkscrewing slipstream.
f3.alt: Left: front view of a high-wing airplane with curved arrows showing the propeller's action one way and the airplane's reaction the other way, with one wingtip arrow pointing down and the other up. Right: a low-wing airplane with the spiraling slipstream wrapping around the fuselage and pushing on the vertical tail, labeled force, with a yaw arrow at the nose.

f4.caption: Figure 11-14. Power required curve.
f4.alt: Graph of power setting versus speed. A U-shaped power required curve sits under a maximum power available line. The low point is best endurance speed; the shaded area to its left is the region of reversed command; the gap between the lines is excess power.

f5.alt: Five airplanes on a runway: premature rotation increases drag, decreases acceleration and increases takeoff distance; airplane may lift off at low airspeed; flight below VX results in shallow climb; airplane may settle back to the ground.

scenario.title: A real grass strip on a warm morning
scenario.setup: Your private-pilot learner has practiced simulated soft-field takeoffs on pavement and today flies to a real turf strip for the first time. The nontowered strip is 2,600 feet long, the grass is still wet from the morning, and there are trees past the departure end. It is warm, and the airplane is near maximum weight with you, the learner and full fuel. The wind sock shows a light quartering wind from the left, and once in a while it swings toward a tailwind. A helicopter operator works from a pad beside the strip, and building cumulus sit 20 miles west. The learner had a long day at work and wants to get the takeoff done before the weather builds.

questions.q: Before you start the engine, what decides whether this strip works today?
questions.a: The POH distance data for today's weight, temperature, elevation, wind and slope [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]], corrected for the surface; the sample chart covers only dry grass [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]], and the RMH case shows a POH with no wet-grass data [[30:64|RMH C-1]]. Add room to stop: takeoff plus landing ground roll [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. If the numbers approach the runway length, the risk is high [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

questions.q: The sock keeps swinging toward a tailwind. How does that change your plan?
questions.a: A tailwind of 10% of takeoff airspeed adds about 21% to takeoff distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. Confirm the POH allows it and the runway is enough [[24:135|AFH 6-3]], or wait for a steady headwind component.

questions.q: How do you brief the crosswind part of the takeoff?
questions.a: Full aileron into the wind at the start [[24:138|AFH 6-6]], and enough held so the airplane sideslips into the wind right after lift-off [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. You will watch drift during the level-off in ground effect and not let it grow beyond the learner's control [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

questions.q: The helicopter starts hover-taxiing near the departure end, and the cumulus are growing. What do you do?
questions.a: Stay at least three rotor diameters from a hovering helicopter and use caution behind a departing one [[34:153|AIM 7-4-7]]. On a soft field, slow acceleration can hide windshear [[28:270|AWH 22-15]], and microburst clues include a rain shaft with virga or a ring of blowing dust [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. If either threat moves closer, wait.

questions.q: What abort and engine-failure plan do you brief?
questions.a: An airborne-by point on the strip; if it is reached on the wheels, power idle, braking with directional control [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. After lift-off: lower the nose at once, coordinate, land ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]; no turn back for a learner [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

questions.q: The learner is tired and rushing. How does that change the flight?
questions.a: External pressure is a hazard; the RMH profile notes a possible external pressure hazard at a turf strip [[30:64|RMH C-1]]. The AIH tells instructors they can change the plan or end a lesson early when a learner is anxious about time pressures [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. A lighter airplane, a later time or another day are all valid mitigations, the same kind of fix the RMH suggests [[30:65|RMH C-2]].

skills.do: Complete the before-takeoff checklist before rolling onto the soft runway, explaining why it must be done before the no-stop lineup.
skills.practice: Run the checklist on firm ground, then brief 'no stopping from here' [[24:133|AFH 6-1]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Make the departure calls, CTAF or tower, and explain the phraseology.
skills.practice: Script a CTAF departure call with the airport name at both ends [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

skills.do: Verify the correct runway and surface before adding power, and say how.
skills.practice: Heading bug on the runway heading; check the turf runway in the Chart Supplement [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]] [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

skills.do: Determine wind direction with or without a wind indicator and teach the learner to read it.
skills.practice: Read the sock, then smoke, dust or water, and compare with the report [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]] [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

skills.do: Position the flight controls for the wind while taxiing and rolling, naming each position.
skills.practice: Call the control position at each taxi turn [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]; full aileron into the wind at the start of the roll [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

skills.do: Clear the area, then taxi into position and align on the centerline without stopping while smoothly advancing to takeoff power, explaining why you keep rolling.
skills.practice: Finish the scan before entering; roll on with enough power and back pressure [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

skills.do: Confirm takeoff power and normal engine and flight instrument indications, saying what you check.
skills.practice: A short gauge callout right after power comes in [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

skills.do: Establish and maintain a pitch attitude that moves the weight from the wheels to the wings as rapidly as possible, explaining the picture.
skills.practice: Back pressure from the start of the roll, then hold the attitude steady [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Lift off at the lowest possible airspeed and stay in ground effect while accelerating to VX or VY, explaining each change.
skills.practice: Lower the nose gently with the wheels just clear; hold it there until VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Establish a pitch attitude for VX or VY, as appropriate, and maintain selected airspeed ±5 knots during the climb (ACS AI.VII.C.S10), while anticipating the pitch-up leaving ground effect.
skills.practice: Attitude first, then a glance at the airspeed [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]; expect the pitch-up [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

skills.do: Configure the airplane after a positive rate of climb or per the manufacturer, and explain the order.
skills.practice: VX until clear, then VY, then gear and flaps, then climb power [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Maintain VX or VY, as appropriate, ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS AI.VII.C.S12) while instructing.
skills.practice: Practice the patter until the talking costs no airspeed; keep prompts short [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

skills.do: Maintain directional control and wind-drift correction through the roll, the level-off in ground effect and the climb.
skills.practice: Rudder for the left-turning effects, aileron into the wind, crab after the climb is established [[24:139|AFH 6-7]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

skills.do: Comply with noise abatement procedures and say where you found them.
skills.practice: Check each strip's procedures; ask the tower when unsure [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common soft-field errors, usually a simulated error flown by the examiner as your 'learner.'
skills.practice: For each AFH error, practice naming what you see, the cause and the fix [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

quiz.q: Which surface does the AFH NOT list as a reason for soft-field takeoff technique?
quiz.why: The AFH names tall grass, soft sand, mud and snow, plus rough fields [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Smooth pavement is where you simulate it, not where you need it.

quiz.q: When should the nose-high attitude be set during a soft-field takeoff roll?
options: As early as possible in the roll
Only after the nosewheel lifts by itself
quiz.why: The weight moves from wheels to wings as rapidly as possible by setting a high angle of attack as early as possible [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

quiz.q: Your POH VX is 63 knots. Which climb airspeed fails the CFI standard but would pass the private standard?
quiz.why: CFI: ±5, 58 to 68 knots (ACS AI.VII.C.S10). Private: +10/-5, 58 to 73 knots (ACS PA.IV.C.S10). Only 71 knots is inside the private window and outside yours.

quiz.q: According to the PHAK, how much is induced drag reduced when the wing is one-tenth of its span above the ground?
quiz.why: 47.6 percent at one-tenth of the span [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. The AFH rounds it to about 50 percent [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: Why is the corkscrew slipstream effect especially strong early in a soft-field roll?
options: The spiral is compact at high propeller speed and low forward speed
The nosewheel is off the ground
quiz.why: At high propeller speeds and low forward speed the spiral is compact and pushes hard on the vertical tail; it elongates as speed builds [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

quiz.q: According to the AIH, when should you do most of the teaching for a takeoff?
options: Before contacting the tower or announcing on CTAF
quiz.why: Teach airspeeds, attitudes, references, control inputs and engine numbers before contacting the tower or announcing on CTAF, to avoid overloading the learner [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

quiz.q: During a learner's soft-field takeoff, what does the AIH single out for the instructor to monitor while the learner tries to stay in ground effect?
quiz.why: Monitor drift and do not let it escalate beyond the learner's control, while watching pitch attitude and airspeed [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

quiz.q: Holding a nosewheel airplane on the ground with forward elevator until VX can cause:
quiz.why: It puts excessive pressure on the nosewheel and may cause wheelbarrowing [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

quiz.q: What may be the only visible clue to a microburst?
options: Smooth air below the cloud base
quiz.why: A ring of blowing dust is often the only visual clue; an intense rain shaft with virga at cloud base may also indicate one [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

quiz.q: Small airplanes should stay at least how far from a helicopter in a slow hover taxi or stationary hover?
quiz.why: Avoid operating within three rotor diameters of a helicopter in a slow hover taxi or stationary hover [[34:153|AIM 7-4-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner holds the soft-field attitude, lifts off, and keeps the same attitude. The airplane rises to about 20 feet and the stall warning chirps. Which AFH error is this, and what is the fix?
options: Lifting off too fast; reduce power
Premature gear retraction; lower the gear
Climbing too high after lift-off and not leveling off low enough; lower the nose and stay in ground effect
Too much rudder; center the ball
final_quiz.why: The AFH lists climbing too high after lift-off and not leveling off low enough to stay in ground effect [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Lower the nose with the wheels clear and accelerate to at least VX in ground effect [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

final_quiz.q: Just after lift-off your learner shoves the yoke forward to level off, and the mains brush the grass. Which AFH error best describes this?
options: Insufficient back pressure in the roll
Abrupt and/or excessive elevator while leveling off
final_quiz.why: Abrupt or excessive elevator control while leveling off and accelerating is a listed error; the AFH says to gently lower the nose [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

final_quiz.q: At VX in ground effect, your learner raises the nose for the climb. The nose keeps rising beyond the planned attitude and the airspeed decays. What did the learner fail to anticipate?
options: The pitch-up as the airplane leaves ground effect, from increased downwash at the tail
The airspeed indicator reading low in ground effect
final_quiz.why: Leaving ground effect gives a pitch-up tendency from increased downwash at the horizontal tail [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]; failing to anticipate it is a listed error [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: Practicing on pavement, your learner pulls the nose so high on the roll that the cowling blocks the runway ahead. What does the AIH guidance say?
options: Nothing; the AIH is silent on soft-field takeoffs
Let the learner discover it, the airplane will lift off anyway
A training scenario must not create an excessive pitch attitude; watch pitch and airspeed and correct it
Higher is better, since it moves more weight to the wings
final_quiz.why: Scenarios should not create an unsafe climb rate or excessive pitch attitude, and during soft-field takeoffs the instructor watches pitch and airspeed throughout [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: Left crosswind. Once airborne in ground effect your learner levels the wings and the airplane drifts right toward the runway edge. What should have been done?
options: Climb out of ground effect immediately
Keep the upwind wing down so the airplane sideslips into the wind right after lift-off
Add right aileron to turn back
Reduce power to settle back on the runway
final_quiz.why: Hold aileron into the wind so the airplane sideslips enough to counteract drift immediately after lift-off [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. The AIH says not to let drift grow beyond the learner's control [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: Why is the AWH's on-the-roll windshear cue less useful on a muddy strip?
options: The cue only works at towered airports
The cue is slow airspeed build-up, and a soft surface already slows acceleration
final_quiz.why: Slower than normal airspeed build-up may be the only sign on the roll [[28:270|AWH 22-15]], and soft surfaces reduce acceleration anyway [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Decide about nearby storms before the roll.

final_quiz.q: Climbing at VX through 30 feet after a soft-field takeoff, you start explaining why VX is slower than VY. What does the AIH say about this?
options: It is the best time, since the learner sees it happen
Explain only if the tower is quiet
Information given during the takeoff may not be heard or processed; teach it on the ground
final_quiz.why: During takeoff the learner's attention is almost all on flying, and information may not be heard or processed; do most teaching before contacting the tower or announcing on CTAF [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: In the RMH accident profile, what single action does the RMH say could have reduced both the environmental and the aircraft performance risk?
options: Departing at night when the air is cooler
Flying solo to a nearby airport and picking the passengers up there
Using a rolling takeoff from a taxiway
Taking off with flaps fully extended
final_quiz.why: Flying the airplane solo to Eugene to board the passengers addresses both risks and the external pressure [[30:65|RMH C-2]].

final_quiz.q: Each time your learner raises the nosewheel abruptly, the nose swings sharply. Which explanation fits the sources?
options: Pitching the propeller produces a yawing moment, and rapid pitch changes give proportionate changes in torque effects
The airspeed indicator is reading low
final_quiz.why: Any pitching gives a yawing moment through gyroscopic action [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]], and excessive, rapid pitch changes cause proportionate changes in torque effects [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. Raise the nose smoothly.

final_quiz.q: At a towered field with a soft turf runway, the tower offers 'line up and wait.' What is the best plan?
options: Line up, stop, and wait with full back pressure
Accept and start the roll, since line up and wait allows it
Begin the roll after 2 minutes if nothing is heard
Hold short until cleared for takeoff so you can roll on without stopping
final_quiz.why: Stopping on a soft surface can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], and line up and wait is not a takeoff clearance [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]]. Holding short until cleared is application of both.

final_quiz.q: Departing a snow-covered strip under an overcast, your learner says, 'I can't tell how high we are,' while holding in ground effect. What is the likely cause?
options: Flat light removing depth perception and contrast
final_quiz.why: Flat light over snow takes away depth and contrast and can give a false sense of climbing or descending [[34:170|AIM 7-6-14]].

final_quiz.q: A warm, humid afternoon at a high grass strip. Which one change would LOWER the density altitude and help your soft-field takeoff?
final_quiz.why: High elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity raise density altitude; low humidity is one of the conditions of low density altitude [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]].

final_quiz.q: After full power on the grass, your learner never looks at the engine gauges until 300 feet. Why does this matter on a soft-field takeoff?
options: It doesn't; the AFH only cares about airspeed
Engine gauges are unreliable in ground effect
Not cross-checking engine instruments after power is a listed error, and a sick engine is a reason to reject while still on the ground
It only matters for turbocharged engines
final_quiz.why: Failure to cross-check engine instruments after applying power is on the soft-field error list [[24:146|AFH 6-14]], and a malfunctioning powerplant is a reason to reject the takeoff [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

takeaways: You hold VX or VY ±5 knots while explaining; your private learner gets +10/-5 (ACS AI.VII.C.S10, PA.IV.C.S10).
Weight to the wings early: back pressure from the first foot of the roll, then hold the attitude [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Lift off slow, level off low, build to VX in ground effect, then climb [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Expect the pitch-up and the settle leaving ground effect; climbing out slow can trap you in reversed command [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Rudder for four left-turning effects at once, and no brakes for steering [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]] [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
Teach on the ground before the radio call; in the air, watch drift, pitch and airspeed [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
A pavement simulation teaches the picture, not the drag: set a pitch limit, then finish on real grass with real numbers.
cfi_notes: The AFH gives the soft-field procedure and error list but no instructor notes [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. The only FAA soft-field teaching line found is in the AIH: monitor drift, pitch and airspeed while the learner stays in ground effect [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

Sources differ slightly on ground effect: the PHAK gives 23.5 and 47.6 percent at one-fourth and one-tenth of the span [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]; the AFH rounds to about 25 and 50 percent [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. Same physics; quote the PHAK when you want the exact numbers.

The sources pull two ways on wind: soft-field says lift off at the lowest possible airspeed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], but in strong gusts the AFH wants an extra margin of speed [[24:137|AFH 6-5]] and in a significant crosswind it holds the mains on longer [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]. Nothing reconciles them. Application: the level-off in ground effect is where you build the margin before climbing; follow the POH.

No source gives a method for simulating a soft field on pavement. The chunk 13 list is application, bounded by the AIH: realistic scenarios, no excessive pitch, realistic imaginary obstacles [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

Flap retraction in increments comes from the AFH short-field section [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]; the soft-field section only says retract after a positive rate and VY [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Figure 6-9 is also from the short-field section.

The RMH text says the Crow-Mag runway was 3,100 feet [[30:64|RMH C-1]], while the chart excerpt shows 30, which reads as about 3,000 feet [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p.15]]. Use the text for the case study and the chart only to teach symbols.

Tailwheel learners (and your own tailwheel endorsement work): keep the tail very low on a soft field and expect a nose-over tendency in soft spots or deep snow; elevator full up while taxiing on [[24:290|AFH 14-4]].
The AFH soft-field error list has typos ('levelng,' 'climb our'). Teach the meaning, not the spelling [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
gaps: Speeds, flap setting, lift-off attitude and whether a soft-field procedure exists at all are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.

No source gives distance corrections for wet grass, mud, snow, slush or sand; the PHAK sample chart covers only dry grass [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]], and the RMH case POH had no wet-turf data [[30:64|RMH C-1]].
No source gives stopping distances or braking data for a rejected takeoff on grass or mud.
No source says how high to hold the nose on pavement or warns about tail clearance in light singles; check the POH and type-specific guidance.
No FAA method for simulating a soft field on a hard runway is in the resources.
AC 00-54 (FAA Pilot Wind Shear Guide), named by the PHAK [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]], is not in the resources.

activities.title: Grass, wind and ground effect math
activities.intro: Use the PHAK sample chart values and notes given in each item, then type your answer.

items.q: Sample chart, 2,400 lb, 4,000 ft, 20 °C: ground roll 1,355 ft. The runway is dry grass. Corrected ground roll?
Same conditions, total to clear 50 ft is 2,570 ft. Add the same dry-grass correction (15% of the ground roll). Corrected total?
items.why: The note adds 15% of the ground roll figure to the distances: 2,570 + 203.25 = 2,773 ft [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

items.q: Sample chart, sea level, 30 °C, paved: ground roll 995 ft. You have a 6-knot tailwind. Ground roll?
Sample chart, 1,000 ft, 40 °C: total to clear 50 ft is 2,155 ft. Headwind 18 knots. Total distance?
Your corrected grass ground roll is 1,558 ft and the POH landing ground roll is 640 ft. Estimate the runway needed to accelerate and then stop.
items.why: Takeoff ground roll plus landing ground roll: 1,558 + 640 = 2,198 ft [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Braking on grass may be worse; no source gives a correction.

items.q: Your wingspan is 34 ft. At what wing height does the PHAK give a 23.5 percent cut in induced drag?

activities.title: True or false: hazards near the surface
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AFH calls the soft-field takeoff procedure quite different from the short-field procedure on firm, smooth surfaces.
A typical microburst is 1 to 2 miles across and about 1,000 feet deep.
cards.why: True: horizontal diameter of 1 to 2 miles and nominal depth of 1,000 feet [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

cards.s: Departing helicopters in forward flight leave no wake worth worrying about.
cards.why: False. They produce a pair of strong, high-speed trailing vortices like larger fixed-wing aircraft [[34:153|AIM 7-4-7]].

cards.s: Flat light happens only over snow.
cards.why: False. It also occurs in dust, sand, mud flats or over glassy water [[34:170|AIM 7-6-14]].

cards.s: Wheelbarrowing comes from too much back-elevator pressure on the takeoff roll.
cards.why: False. It comes from weight concentrated on the nosewheel, such as forward elevator pressure [[24:144|AFH 6-12]] [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

cards.s: Most midair collisions in the AIH study happened at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet.

activities.title: Teaching it on pavement
activities.intro: Your private learner flies normal takeoffs well. Today you introduce the soft-field takeoff on a long paved runway at a towered airport, with a light left crosswind.

steps.s: Before the flight, what goes into the soft-field briefing?
options: Attitudes, airspeeds, references, control inputs, the 'runway is soft' rules and a realistic imaginary obstacle
Nothing; you will explain it on the roll
A list of regulations about grass strips
steps.why: Teach the airspeeds, attitudes, references and control inputs before the radio call, and make the scenario realistic, with a realistic imaginary obstacle [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

steps.s: At the hold line, tower says 'line up and wait.' What do you do?
options: Accept and stop on the centerline
Ask to hold short until you can be cleared for takeoff, so the learner practices the rolling entry
Begin the roll without a clearance
steps.why: The soft-field lineup keeps moving [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], and line up and wait is not a takeoff clearance [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]]. Holding short is application of both.

steps.s: On the roll the learner's nose comes up so high that the runway ahead disappears under the cowling. You say:
options: 'Lower it a little, hold this attitude'
steps.why: A training scenario must not create an excessive pitch attitude, and you watch pitch and airspeed throughout [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

steps.s: Airborne a few feet up, the airplane is drifting right toward the runway edge and the learner has not noticed.
options: Prompt 'left wing down into the wind, rudder to stay straight' and be ready to take the controls
Let it drift so they learn
Tell them to climb out of ground effect
steps.why: Hold aileron into the wind to sideslip against the drift [[24:139|AFH 6-7]], and do not let the drift escalate beyond the learner's control [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

steps.s: Climbing at VX, the imaginary obstacle not yet passed, the learner reaches for the flap switch.
options: Allow it, it helps the climb
'Eyes outside. Flaps stay until we're clear and at VY'
steps.why: Climb at VX until the obstacle is cleared, then VY, then retract [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]; keep focus outside until obstacles are cleared [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].
